I am leaving my full-time job and becoming an independent I.T. consultant/contractor. AMA
In which country are you working/planning to work? It'll help frame the mind-set of questions.
What made you decide to take this step, and what are your contingency plans?
What's the most disastrous mistake you have ever made on a job?

Hi there! Much respect for making the transition. It's my dream to be my own boss one day but I'm worried about failing and going into debt. You said you are leaving your full time job. So I assume you have insurance, stock, bonuses, 401k, etc with your company. So my question is, do you have a plan to hopefully not only replace your salary but also maintain these additional full time benefits? If so, can you share some insight on how you plan to do so? Will you incorporate for tax purposes?

What made you finally decide on this? I'm graduating in a year and am the type of person who doesn't want to work in a full-time job my whole life and to become independent. Is there any way I can learn from you as I go through this?

Edit: I forgot a big one: Form an LLC. It depends on the state, but here in Ohio it only costs $125 and the form is just a couple of pages. This protects your personal assets from a lawsuit. Not that it's gonna happen, but if somebody's server explodes and they lose data they could still try blaming you. All business you do needs to be done as the LLC, not yourself personally.

I did this for a couple of years but ended up going back to a full time job for the sake of stability. Here's a couple of thoughts:

  1. Put 30% of every dollar you make aside for taxes. It would be good to have a relationship with an accountant from the get go to make sure every is kept track of.
  2. You'll need to figure out what you need to do health insurance-wise since it's required now. I just did without so I'm not exactly sure what the requirements are.
  3. When you're out selling, try to get people set up with managed services contracts. It creates a regular revenue stream regardless of the client having problems.
  4. Find somebody else doing what you do and have an agreement with them to be your backup (and maybe be theirs). You never know if you'll have two emergencies at once. Or your car breaks down. Or you had to take your mom to the doctor and won't be done until 2:00 but an Exchange server went down. This will also let you sell yourself as if you're more than one person. I found that the one person thing was kind of a turn off, especially to companies with more than just a handful of people. That said:
  5. Try to find at least one client that's got a good 25 - 30 people. Something that will generate some revenue but not be too big to handle yourself. In my case it was a law firm with about 50 people. Unfortunately they broke up and split into multiple firms and the couple that stuck with me didn't amount to much so I said screw it and got a real job again.
  6. Have a good looking website, and email at your own domain. And nice looking business cards. juscelino@hotmail.com won't cut it. Personally I was using gotprint.com for cards. It's only $12 for 1000 glossy color cards. The selling part is all about the image.
What kind of qualifications do you have? I have a lot of experience in IT and considered jumping to a consultant role instead, but I am not sure I would be qualified enough to match the competition.
